sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
### Bringing murmurs out

- **Mitral stenosis**: left lateral decubitus, bell lightly on the apex, after a few sit-ups (tachycardia increases flow).
- **Aortic regurgitation**: sitting up and leaning forward, breath held in **expiration**, diaphragm along the left sternal edge.
- **Right-sided murmurs**: listen during **inspiration**.
- **Carotid radiation**: listen over both carotids (AS radiates; a carotid bruit is louder higher in the neck).

### Innocent murmurs

An innocent (functional) murmur is **systolic**, **soft (grade 1-2)**, **short** and early-to-mid systolic, localised, with **normal S1 and S2** (normal splitting), **no click, no thrill**, normal pulses and apex, and it changes with posture. Examples: Still's vibratory murmur in children, pulmonary flow murmur, the venous hum (continuous) and the mammary souffle of pregnancy.

**Needs an echocardiogram:** any **diastolic** murmur (other than a venous hum), a **holosystolic** or late systolic murmur, grade 3 or more, a thrill, an abnormal S2, a click, or symptoms.
sections.title: Physical examination

sections.body:
### Grading (Levine)

| Grade | Description |
|---|---|
| 1 | Very faint; heard only after the listener has "tuned in", not in all positions |
| 2 | Quiet but heard immediately the stethoscope is placed |
| 3 | Moderately loud; **no thrill** |
| 4 | Loud, **with a thrill** |
| 5 | Very loud, thrill; heard with only the **edge** of the stethoscope on the chest |
| 6 | Heard with the stethoscope **just off** the chest; thrill |

Diastolic murmurs are usually graded 1-4. **Loudness reflects the gradient and the flow, not the severity**: a tiny VSD can be grade 5, and severe AS with a failing ventricle can be grade 2.

### The classic murmurs

| Lesion | Timing and shape | Site and radiation | Key companions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aortic stenosis | Ejection, crescendo-decrescendo, harsh; **later peak = more severe** | Right 2nd ICS -> **carotids** (may reach the apex: Gallavardin) | Slow-rising pulse, soft A2, heaving apex, S4 |
| HCM (obstructive) | Ejection, harsh | LLSB/apex, **no carotid radiation** | Jerky pulse, double apex, louder on Valsalva |
| Mitral regurgitation | Holosystolic plateau, blowing | Apex -> **axilla** (anterior jets of posterior-leaflet prolapse radiate to the base) | Soft S1, S3, displaced apex |
| VSD | Holosystolic, harsh | LLSB (3rd-4th ICS), localised, thrill | Normal S1; loudness inverse to defect size |
| Tricuspid regurgitation | Holosystolic | LLSB, **louder on inspiration (Carvallo)** | Giant cv waves, pulsatile liver |
| Mitral valve prolapse | Mid-systolic click + late systolic murmur | Apex | Moves earlier on standing |
| Aortic regurgitation | Early diastolic decrescendo, high-pitched, blowing | Left sternal edge (3rd-4th ICS); **right** edge if the root is dilated | Collapsing pulse, wide pulse pressure |
| Pulmonary regurgitation | Early diastolic decrescendo | Left 2nd-3rd ICS, louder on inspiration | Loud P2 if pulmonary hypertension (Graham Steell) |
| Mitral stenosis | Mid-diastolic rumble, low-pitched, presystolic accentuation in sinus rhythm | Apex, **localised**, left lateral position, bell | Loud S1, opening snap |
| PDA | Continuous "machinery", peaks at S2 | Left infraclavicular | Collapsing pulse |

sections.title: Murmur

sections.body:
Work through the decision tree below: timing first, then shape, then site and radiation, then the response to manoeuvres, then the companion signs that point to the lesion and its severity.

[[figure:pe-murmur-identification-algorithm]]

**Severity at the bedside:**

| Lesion | Signs of severity |
|---|---|
| AS | Slow-rising small pulse, **late peak**, soft or absent A2 (single or paradoxically split S2), S4, LV heave, signs of failure |
| MR | Displaced apex, **S3**, wide split S2 (early A2), mid-diastolic flow rumble |
| AR | **Long** murmur, wide pulse pressure with low diastolic pressure, displaced apex, Austin Flint murmur, S3 |
| MS | **Short A2-OS interval**, **long rumble**, signs of pulmonary hypertension (loud P2, RV heave, Graham Steell) |
| PS | Long murmur peaking late, click close to S1, soft delayed P2, RV heave, giant a wave |
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
- **Loudness is not severity.** Severe AS with low flow can be soft; a small VSD can be loud.
- The **Gallavardin phenomenon**: the musical high-frequency part of an AS murmur heard at the apex can mimic MR; MR does not vary with cycle length after a pause, AS does.
- **Acute severe MR and acute severe AR have short, soft murmurs** (early pressure equalisation); do not be reassured by a quiet murmur in a shocked patient.
- Every **diastolic** murmur and every continuous murmur except the venous hum and mammary souffle is pathological.
- The mid-diastolic rumble of **Austin Flint** (severe AR) has no opening snap and no loud S1.
- A to-and-fro murmur (AS + AR) is **not** a continuous murmur: there is a gap at S2.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Ejection systolic murmur at the right 2nd ICS radiating to the carotids, soft A2" -> severe AS.
- "Pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, soft S1, S3" -> chronic MR.
- "Harsh pansystolic murmur at the LLSB with a thrill in a child" -> VSD.
- "Early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, sitting forward" -> AR.
- "Low-pitched apical rumble with presystolic accentuation" -> MS in sinus rhythm.
- "Continuous machinery murmur under the left clavicle" -> PDA.
- "Grade 2 short systolic murmur, normal S2, asymptomatic child" -> innocent murmur.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Describe: **timing, shape, site, radiation, grade, pitch, manoeuvres, companions**.
- Levine: **grade 4 = thrill**; 5 = stethoscope edge; 6 = off the chest.
- AS -> carotids; MR -> axilla; AR -> left sternal edge (right edge if root disease); MS -> localised at the apex.
- Later-peaking AS murmur, shorter A2-OS, longer AR murmur = more severe.
- Diastolic, holosystolic, grade 3 or more, thrill, abnormal S2 or a click = not innocent: echo.

sections.body: A **narrow-complex tachycardia** has a rate over 100/min and a QRS under 120 ms, which means the ventricles are activated through the His-Purkinje system: the rhythm originates **above the bifurcation of the His bundle** (supraventricular). The two questions that classify it are **regular or irregular?** and **where is the P wave?** (the RP and PR relation).
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
- **Sinus tachycardia** and **focal atrial tachycardia**: enhanced automaticity (or triggered activity); rate warms up and cools down.
- **Atrial fibrillation**: multiple wavelets with rotor or focal (pulmonary-vein) drivers; the AV node filters chaotic input, giving an irregularly irregular ventricular response.
- **Typical atrial flutter**: a macro-re-entrant circuit around the tricuspid annulus through the cavotricuspid isthmus (counter-clockwise), cycle length about 200 ms (atrial rate about 300/min).
- **AVNRT**: re-entry within the AV node region using slow and fast pathways; in the typical (slow-fast) form atria and ventricles are activated almost simultaneously, so the P wave hides in or just after the QRS.
- **AVRT**: re-entry using an accessory pathway. *Orthodromic* (about 90-95%): down the AV node, up the pathway - narrow QRS, P after the QRS. *Antidromic*: down the pathway - wide, pre-excited QRS.

Re-entry and automaticity are covered on the Physiology II page **"Mechanisms of arrhythmia"**; the vector basis of P-wave polarity is on **"ECG genesis: vectors, intervals and axis"**.
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
[[figure:ecg-af-strip]]

[[figure:ecg-flutter-2to1-strip]]

[[figure:ecg-avnrt-strip]]

Rhythm | Regularity | Atrial activity | Clue
---|---|---|---
Sinus tachycardia | Regular | Normal P before each QRS | Gradual onset; cause (fever, pain, hypovolaemia, PE)
Atrial fibrillation | Irregularly irregular | No P; fibrillatory waves | Ventricular rate varies beat to beat
Atrial flutter | Regular (or regularly irregular with variable block) | Sawtooth F waves about 300/min, negative in II/III/aVF, positive V1 | **Rate 150 = flutter 2:1 until proven otherwise**
Multifocal atrial tachycardia | Irregular | 3 or more P morphologies, variable PR | COPD, hypoxia, low K/Mg
Typical AVNRT | Regular, abrupt onset/offset | P hidden or at the end of QRS: pseudo-S in II/III/aVF, pseudo-r' in V1 | RP under 70 ms
Orthodromic AVRT | Regular | Retrograde P in the ST segment | RP 70 ms or more, RP shorter than PR; sinus ECG shows pre-excitation only if the pathway is manifest (normal with a concealed pathway)
Focal atrial tachycardia / PJRT / atypical AVNRT | Regular | P before QRS, abnormal axis | **Long RP** (RP longer than PR)

**Pre-excitation in sinus rhythm (WPW pattern)**: short PR (under 120 ms), a **delta wave** (slurred QRS upstroke) and a wide QRS with secondary ST-T change. "WPW syndrome" = the pattern plus arrhythmia. Delta-wave polarity localises the pathway: negative delta in I and aVL with a positive delta in V1 points to a left lateral pathway; a negative delta in V1 with left axis suggests a right-sided pathway.

[[figure:ecg-wpw-12-lead]]
sections.title: ECG

sections.body:
**Unstable** (shock, syncope, ischaemia, acute heart failure): synchronised DC cardioversion, whatever the mechanism.

**Stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia (ESC 2019 SVT):**
1. **Vagal manoeuvres** - the modified Valsalva (strain, then lie flat with the legs raised) is the most effective.
2. **IV adenosine** (6 mg, then 12 mg, then 18 mg if needed, each as a rapid bolus with flush, while recording a rhythm strip). It terminates AV-node-dependent tachycardias (AVNRT, AVRT) and unmasks flutter waves or atrial tachycardia by transient AV block. Warn about flushing and chest tightness; caution in severe asthma; heart transplant and dipyridamole increase the effect.
3. IV verapamil or diltiazem (avoid if hypotensive or LV dysfunction) or an IV beta-blocker.
4. Synchronised cardioversion if drugs fail.
5. Long term: **catheter ablation** is first-line for recurrent symptomatic AVNRT, AVRT and typical flutter.

**Atrial fibrillation (ESC 2024)**: anticoagulation decided by **CHA2DS2-VA** (2 or more: recommended; 1: should be considered), rate control (beta-blocker; diltiazem/verapamil if LVEF over 40%; digoxin), and rhythm control for symptoms or early AF.

**Pre-excited AF** (irregular, very fast, varying QRS width): **avoid AV-nodal blockers** (adenosine, verapamil/diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin), which can accelerate conduction down the pathway into VF. Use synchronised cardioversion if unstable, IV procainamide or ibutilide if stable, then ablation.
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body:
- **Regular tachycardia at 150/min** with "no P waves": look for a second flutter wave hidden in the T wave or QRS; adenosine reveals it.
- **AF that suddenly becomes regular** is not AF any more: think flutter or atrial tachycardia, or complete heart block with a junctional/ventricular escape or accelerated junctional rhythm (digoxin toxicity).
- **Adenosine in pre-excited AF** or **verapamil in an undiagnosed wide tachycardia** can be fatal.
- **Sinus tachycardia is not treated with rate control**: treat the cause (sepsis, hypovolaemia, PE).
- **Short PR alone** without a delta wave is not WPW.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Sudden palpitations, regular 180/min, pseudo-r' in V1, terminated by adenosine" = typical AVNRT.
- "Ventricular rate exactly 150" = flutter with 2:1 block.
- "Young patient, AF at 250/min with bizarre wide complexes" = pre-excited AF: procainamide or cardioversion, never verapamil.
- Delta wave + short PR + palpitations = WPW syndrome: refer for ablation.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Narrow QRS = supraventricular origin; classify by regularity and RP interval.
- RP under 70 ms: typical AVNRT; RP 70 ms or more, short RP: orthodromic AVRT; long RP: atrial tachycardia, PJRT, atypical AVNRT.
- Flutter: sawtooth, negative in inferior leads, 300/min; 2:1 gives 150/min; CTI ablation first-line for recurrence.
- Acute SVT: modified Valsalva, then adenosine; ablation for long-term cure.
- Pre-excited AF: no AV-nodal blockers.

sections.body: This page gathers the patterns that are not primary rhythm or coronary problems but appear in almost every exam: **acute pericarditis** (and how to separate it from STEMI and early repolarisation), **pericardial effusion and tamponade**, **acute pulmonary embolism**, **paced rhythms** and a few classic "spot diagnoses" (hypothermia, raised intracranial pressure, dextrocardia).
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
**Acute pericarditis.** Inflammation of the epicardium produces a diffuse injury current. ECG changes are present in most patients and evolve through four stages (Spodick): **stage I** diffuse concave ST elevation with **PR depression** (and the mirror in aVR: ST depression and PR elevation); **stage II** ST and PR normalise, T flattens; **stage III** diffuse T inversion; **stage IV** normalisation. Sinus tachycardia is common. Q waves do not develop. Why aVR shows the mirror image (its lead axis points away from the apex and lateral wall, towards which the diffuse injury current is directed) follows from the lead vectors on the Physiology II page **"ECG genesis: vectors, intervals and axis"**.

[[figure:ecg-pericarditis-12-lead]]

Feature | Acute pericarditis | STEMI | Benign early repolarisation
---|---|---|---
Distribution | Diffuse, not one territory | Coronary territory | Mainly V2-V5 (and inferior)
ST shape | Concave | Convex / straight; hyperacute T | Concave with J-point notch or slur
Reciprocal ST depression | Only aVR (and V1) | Yes | No
PR depression | Yes (in most) | No | No
Q waves | No | Develop | No
T inversion | After ST returns to baseline | While ST still elevated | No
Evolution | Days to weeks | Hours | Stable over years
ST/T ratio in V6 | Over 0.25 | - | Under 0.25

**Pericardial effusion / tamponade**: **low QRS voltage** (under 5 mm in all limb leads, under 10 mm in all chest leads), sinus tachycardia and **electrical alternans** (beat-to-beat alternation of QRS amplitude from the heart swinging in the fluid). Low voltage + tachycardia + alternans = tamponade until proven otherwise: urgent echocardiography and pericardiocentesis. Other causes of low voltage: obesity, emphysema, hypothyroidism, infiltrative cardiomyopathy (amyloid: low voltage despite a thick LV), large MI.

**Acute pulmonary embolism**: the most common finding is **sinus tachycardia**; signs of acute RV strain are present in a minority and are insensitive: **S1Q3T3** (deep S in I, Q and inverted T in III), new **RBBB** (complete or incomplete), **right axis** shift, **T inversion in V1-V4** (often with III and aVF), right atrial enlargement, AF. RV-strain signs are associated with more severe PE, but the ECG neither confirms nor excludes PE; diagnosis rests on pre-test probability, D-dimer and CT pulmonary angiography (or echo in the unstable patient).

**Paced rhythms.** Spikes precede the paced chamber. **RV apical pacing**: wide LBBB-like QRS with a superior (left) axis and discordant ST-T. **Biventricular pacing**: a narrower QRS, often a dominant R in V1 and a negative QRS in lead I (rightward axis). **His/left-bundle-area pacing**: near-normal QRS. Problems: **failure to capture** (spike with no P or QRS), **failure to sense / undersensing** (spikes in inappropriate places, risk of R-on-T), **oversensing** (pauses without spikes), pacemaker-mediated tachycardia. Ischaemia in RV pacing: use the Sgarbossa/Smith criteria as in LBBB. Pacing modes and indications are in the ESC 2021 pacing guideline (see the AV-block page).

**Other spot diagnoses**
- **Hypothermia**: bradycardia, long intervals, **Osborn (J) waves** at the QRS-ST junction, shivering artefact, AF.
- **Raised intracranial pressure / subarachnoid haemorrhage**: giant inverted ("cerebral") T waves, long QT, bradycardia.
- **Dextrocardia**: inverted P, QRS and T in I, upright aVR, **decreasing R waves from V1 to V6** (versus LA/RA reversal, where chest leads are normal).
- **Arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy**: T inversion V1-V3, **epsilon wave** (small notch after the QRS in V1-V3), RV-origin (LBBB-shaped) PVCs or VT.
- **Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy**: LVH voltage, deep narrow septal Q waves in lateral and inferior leads; apical HCM gives giant T inversion in V2-V5.
sections.title: ECG

sections.body:
- **Pericarditis (ESC 2015; ESC 2025 myocarditis and pericarditis guidelines)**: diagnose with 2 of 4 criteria (pericarditic chest pain, friction rub, new widespread ST elevation or PR depression, new or worsening effusion; ESC 2025 adds raised CRP and CMR evidence of pericardial inflammation as supporting criteria); treat with high-dose aspirin or an NSAID plus **colchicine** (reduces recurrence), exercise restriction; check troponin (myopericarditis) and echo for effusion. Corticosteroids are second-line.
- **Tamponade**: urgent pericardiocentesis; avoid diuretics and vasodilators.
- **PE**: risk stratification by haemodynamics, RV dysfunction and troponin; anticoagulation, systemic thrombolysis for high-risk (shock) PE.
- **Pacemaker malfunction**: check the battery and lead (chest X-ray, device interrogation), magnet for oversensing inhibition, temporary pacing if pacing-dependent with loss of capture.
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body:
- **ST elevation everywhere is not always pericarditis**: an extensive anterior STEMI (proximal LAD wrapping the apex) or left main occlusion can look diffuse - look for reciprocal depression and convexity.
- **T inversion with ST still elevated** favours infarction; in pericarditis T inverts only after ST normalises.
- **S1Q3T3 is neither sensitive nor specific** for PE; most PE ECGs show only sinus tachycardia.
- **Electrical alternans** also occurs in some tachycardias (AVRT) without effusion.
- **Pacing spikes are small in bipolar pacing** and may be missed; an LBBB-like QRS with a superior axis in a patient with a device should prompt a careful look.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Young man after a viral illness, pleuritic pain relieved by sitting forward, diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression" = acute pericarditis: NSAID + colchicine.
- "Hypotension, raised JVP, low voltage, electrical alternans" = tamponade: pericardiocentesis.
- "Post-operative dyspnoea, sinus tachycardia, new RBBB, T inversion V1-V4" = acute PE with RV strain.
- "Spikes not followed by QRS after a fall" = loss of capture (lead dislodgement).
- "Hypothermic patient with J waves" = Osborn waves.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Pericarditis: diffuse concave ST elevation + PR depression, mirror in aVR, no Q, no reciprocal depression; T inverts only after ST normalises.
- Tamponade triad on ECG: tachycardia, low voltage, electrical alternans.
- PE: sinus tachycardia most common; S1Q3T3, RBBB, right axis, T inversion V1-V4 suggest RV strain.
- RV pacing: LBBB-like with left axis; look for capture and sensing failures.
- Osborn waves = hypothermia; epsilon wave = ARVC; giant inverted T = raised ICP or apical HCM.

title: Pericarditis, pulmonary embolism, pacing and other patterns

sections.body: **Chronic severe aortic regurgitation** produces the richest set of peripheral signs in cardiology, because a large stroke volume is ejected into the aorta (high systolic pressure) and then runs back into the LV and out to the periphery in diastole (low diastolic pressure). The result is a **wide pulse pressure** and a **hyperdynamic circulation** that makes arteries, capillaries and even the head and uvula pulsate. Most of the eponymous signs are simply visible, palpable or audible consequences of this wide pulse pressure, so they also occur in other **high-output or run-off states** (PDA, AV fistula, thyrotoxicosis, anaemia, pregnancy, beriberi, Paget disease).
sections.title: Definition

sections.body: **Chronic vs acute AR.** In chronic AR the LV dilates slowly (eccentric hypertrophy) and can eject a huge stroke volume: wide pulse pressure, displaced hyperdynamic apex, florid peripheral signs. In **acute severe AR** (endocarditis, dissection, trauma) the normal-sized LV cannot dilate: LV diastolic pressure rises steeply and **equalises with the aortic diastolic pressure**, so the murmur is **short and soft**, S1 is soft (early mitral closure), the pulse pressure is **not** wide and the peripheral signs are **absent**; the patient is tachycardic, in pulmonary oedema or shock. An absent sign does not exclude severe AR.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body:
### The eponymous signs of aortic regurgitation

| Sign | What you find |
|---|---|
| **Corrigan sign / pulse** | Visible forceful carotid pulsation with rapid collapse; the collapsing (water-hammer) pulse |
| **de Musset sign** | Head nodding in time with each heartbeat |
| **Quincke sign** | Visible capillary pulsation in the nail bed (press lightly on the nail tip) or lips |
| **Traube sign** | "Pistol-shot" sounds heard over the femoral artery (systolic, sometimes systolic and diastolic) |
| **Duroziez sign** | Over the femoral artery with gentle stethoscope compression: a systolic murmur when compressed proximally and a **diastolic** murmur when compressed distally (reversed diastolic flow) |
| **Muller (Müller) sign** | Systolic pulsation of the uvula |
| **Hill sign** | Popliteal (leg) systolic pressure much higher than brachial systolic pressure |
| **Mayne sign** | Fall in diastolic pressure when the arm is raised |
| **Becker sign** | Visible pulsation of the retinal arteries |
| **Landolfi sign** | Pupillary constriction and dilatation with each beat |
| **Gerhardt / Rosenbach signs** | Pulsatile spleen / pulsatile liver |

[[figure:pe-pulse-collapsing]]

[[figure:pe-pulse-bisferiens]]

**Pulse and pressure:** collapsing pulse (best felt with the arm raised, palm on the radial), sometimes **bisferiens**; wide pulse pressure with a **low diastolic pressure**; Korotkoff sounds may be heard down to near 0 (record phase IV).
sections.title: Peripheral pulse

sections.body:
### The auscultatory signs

- **Early diastolic decrescendo murmur**: high-pitched, blowing, at the **left** sternal edge (3rd-4th ICS) with the patient leaning forward in held expiration; louder at the **right** sternal edge when the cause is **aortic root** dilatation (Marfan, dissection, syphilis). Its **duration**, not its loudness, tracks severity.
- **Systolic ejection (flow) murmur** at the base from the large stroke volume, even without stenosis: a to-and-fro murmur.
- **Austin Flint murmur**: an apical mid-to-late diastolic rumble in severe AR (the jet impinges on the anterior mitral leaflet). No opening snap, no loud S1, softer with amyl nitrite.
- **S3** and a **soft S1** in advanced or acute disease.

[[figure:pe-phono-aortic-regurgitation]]
sections.title: Murmur

sections.body:
### Other eponymous signs the exam asks about

| Eponym | Finding | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Austin Flint** | Apical diastolic rumble | Severe AR |
| **Graham Steell** | Early diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge, louder on inspiration | Pulmonary regurgitation from pulmonary hypertension (classically MS) |
| **Carvallo** | Holosystolic murmur louder on inspiration | Tricuspid regurgitation |
| **Gallavardin** | AS murmur heard musical at the apex | Aortic stenosis mimicking MR |
| **Kussmaul sign** | JVP rises on inspiration | Constriction, restrictive cardiomyopathy, RV infarction |
| **Kussmaul (pulsus paradoxus)** | Pulse weakens on inspiration | Tamponade (Kussmaul named the paradox) |
| **Friedreich sign** | Steep y descent | Constrictive pericarditis |
| **Beck triad** | Hypotension, raised JVP, quiet heart sounds | Acute tamponade |
| **Ewart sign** | Dullness and bronchial breathing below the left scapula | Large pericardial effusion |
| **Broadbent sign** | Systolic retraction of the left posterior chest wall | Constrictive pericarditis (pericardial adhesions) |
| **Lancisi sign** | Giant systolic (cv) waves in the neck | Severe TR |
| **Osler, Janeway, Roth** | Painful pulp nodules, painless palmar macules, retinal haemorrhages | Infective endocarditis |
| **Brockenbrough-Braunwald-Morrow** | Smaller pulse pressure after a premature beat | Obstructive HCM |
| **Means-Lerman scratch** | Systolic scratch at the left upper sternal edge | Thyrotoxicosis |
| **Hamman sign** | Crunching sound synchronous with the heartbeat | Pneumomediastinum |
| **Carey Coombs** | Soft mid-diastolic apical murmur | Acute rheumatic carditis |
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
- The peripheral signs reflect a **wide pulse pressure**, not AR itself: PDA, AV fistula, thyrotoxicosis and pregnancy can produce them.
- **Acute severe AR has no peripheral signs** and a short soft murmur; do not use their absence to exclude it.
- **Duroziez**: the diagnostic component is the **diastolic** murmur on **distal** compression; a systolic murmur alone is normal with heavy compression.
- **Kussmaul's name is on two signs**: pulsus paradoxus (tamponade) and the inspiratory rise of the JVP (constriction).
- An AR murmur loudest at the **right** sternal edge suggests **aortic root disease**, including dissection.
- **Austin Flint vs MS**: no opening snap, no loud S1, softer with amyl nitrite.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Head bobbing with each heartbeat" -> de Musset sign (AR).
- "Capillary pulsation in the nail bed" -> Quincke sign.
- "Pistol-shot femoral sounds" -> Traube sign; "diastolic femoral murmur on distal compression" -> Duroziez sign.
- "Pulsating uvula" -> Muller sign.
- "Leg systolic pressure much higher than arm pressure" -> Hill sign, severe AR.
- "Apical diastolic rumble in a patient with a collapsing pulse" -> Austin Flint murmur.
- "Early diastolic murmur louder on the right with tearing chest pain" -> aortic dissection with AR.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Chronic severe AR: **wide pulse pressure** -> Corrigan, de Musset, Quincke, Traube, Duroziez, Muller, Hill.
- **Duration** of the AR murmur and a **low diastolic pressure** track severity; Austin Flint and S3 mean severe AR.
- **Acute AR**: short soft murmur, soft S1, no widening of pulse pressure, no peripheral signs, shock.
- Right sternal edge AR murmur = root disease or dissection.
- Know the pairs: Graham Steell (PR in PH), Carvallo (TR), Friedreich (constriction), Ewart (effusion), Gallavardin (AS).

title: Peripheral signs of aortic regurgitation and other eponymous cardiovascular signs

sections.body:
Cardiac cells generate two kinds of action potential (AP):
- **Fast-response** APs in atrial and ventricular myocytes and the **His-Purkinje** system - driven by a fast Na+ upstroke, with a stable resting potential (~ -90 mV).
- **Slow-response** APs in the **SA and AV nodes** - driven by Ca2+, with no stable resting potential; instead they depolarise spontaneously (**automaticity**), making them pacemakers.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
**Fast-response AP - phases 0-4:**
- **Phase 0** - rapid depolarisation; fast **Na+ influx (INa)**; upstroke to ~ +20 mV.
- **Phase 1** - early partial repolarisation; **transient outward K+ (Ito)**.
- **Phase 2 (plateau)** - the hallmark of cardiac muscle; inward **L-type Ca2+ (ICaL)** balances outward **K+ (IK)**; sustains contraction and the long refractory period.
- **Phase 3** - repolarisation; K+ efflux (**IKr, IKs**) dominates as Ca2+ channels close.
- **Phase 4** - resting potential ~ -90 mV, held by **IK1** and the Na/K-ATPase.

**Slow-response (pacemaker) AP:**
- **Phase 4** - spontaneous diastolic depolarisation from the **"funny" current (If, Na+)** plus T-type Ca2+, drifting from the maximum diastolic potential (~ -60 mV) up to threshold (~ -40 mV). The **rate of this slope sets heart rate** (sympathetic steepens it, vagal flattens it).
- **Phase 0** - slow upstroke carried by **L-type Ca2+ (ICaL)**, not Na+ - which is why it is slower and why nodal conduction is Ca2+-dependent.
- **Phase 3** - K+ efflux repolarises. (No distinct phases 1-2.)

[[figure:action-potential]]

**Refractory periods:** during the **effective refractory period (ERP)** no stimulus can trigger a new AP (Na+ channels inactivated); the long plateau makes cardiac ERP very long, **preventing tetany**. In fast-response tissue, recovery is **voltage- and time-dependent** (channels reset on repolarisation); in nodal tissue it is largely **time-dependent**, so nodes recover slowly and show **decremental conduction** at fast rates (protecting the ventricle in AF/flutter).
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
**Conduction system and intrinsic rates** (each lower pacemaker is a slower backup; a faster one overdrive-suppresses the rest):
- **SA node - 60-100/min** (dominant pacemaker).
- **AV node - 40-60/min**; conducts **slowest (~0.05 m/s)**, creating the **AV delay (~0.1 s)** so the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract (the atrial kick).
- **His-Purkinje / ventricle - 20-40/min**; Purkinje conducts **fastest (~2-4 m/s)** for near-simultaneous ventricular activation.

[[figure:conduction-system]]

Sequence: **SA node -> atria -> AV node -> bundle of His -> right & left bundle branches -> Purkinje fibres -> ventricular myocardium.**
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body:
The surface ECG is the body-surface summation of these events:
- **P wave** = atrial depolarisation.
- **PR interval (0.12-0.20 s)** = onset of atrial depolarisation to onset of ventricular depolarisation - dominated by the **AV nodal delay**.
- **QRS (< 0.12 s)** = ventricular depolarisation (via His-Purkinje).
- **ST segment** = phase 2 plateau (isoelectric; all ventricular cells depolarised).
- **T wave** = ventricular repolarisation (phase 3).
- **QT interval** = total ventricular AP duration (depolarisation + repolarisation); prolonged by drugs/electrolytes that delay phase-3 K+ efflux (risk of torsades).
sections.title: ECG

sections.body: Electrophysiology is where arrhythmias, antiarrhythmic drugs, pacing and the ECG all originate. Knowing which ion drives each phase, which tissue paces at what rate, and how refractoriness and the AV delay protect the ventricle lets you reason out mechanisms of blocks, re-entry, and drug effects rather than memorising them.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **Nodal upstroke is Ca2+, not Na+** - a favourite distractor; this is why Ca-channel blockers and the Ca-dependent AV node slow the rate.
- The **resting/phase-4 potential of pacemakers is unstable** (that is the whole point) - they have **no true resting potential**.
- Phase 2 is the **plateau (Ca2+ in = K+ out)**, not rapid repolarisation.
- **IK1 maintains the resting potential**; it is a potassium current, not sodium.
- A slower pacemaker does not "fail" - it is **overdrive-suppressed** by the faster SA node until that fails (then escape rhythms at the lower rates).
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Ion responsible for phase 0 of the SA node?" -> **Ca2+ (L-type)**. For ventricular myocyte -> **Na+**.
- "What sets heart rate at the SA node?" -> **slope of phase-4 depolarisation (If)**.
- A conduction-velocity ranking -> **AV node slowest, Purkinje fastest**.
- "Why the PR interval / AV delay?" -> lets **atrial contraction complete before ventricular systole**.
- ECG-to-AP mapping (ST = plateau, T = repolarisation, QT = total AP duration).
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **Phase 0 fast AP = Na+; phase 0 nodal AP = Ca2+.** Plateau (phase 2) = Ca2+ in.
- **Pacemaker phase-4 slope (If) sets heart rate**; steeper with sympathetic, flatter with vagal tone.
- Intrinsic rates: **SA 60-100, AV 40-60, Purkinje/ventricle 20-40/min.**
- **AV node = slowest conduction (the PR delay); Purkinje = fastest.**
- The long plateau -> long **ERP -> no tetany**; nodal refractoriness is time-dependent -> **decremental conduction** protects the ventricle in atrial tachyarrhythmias.
- ECG map: **P = atrial depol, PR = AV delay, QRS = ventricular depol, T = ventricular repol, QT = total AP.**
sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: Cardiac action potentials & conduction

sections.body:
**Afterload** is the load the ventricle must overcome to eject blood - more precisely, the **wall stress (tension) developed during ejection**. It is the resistance/impedance *opposing* ventricular shortening, in contrast to preload, which is the stretch *before* contraction.

Clinically it is approximated by **systolic arterial pressure** or **systemic vascular resistance (SVR)**, but the quantity the myocyte actually "feels" is **wall stress**, which also depends on chamber size and wall thickness.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
Wall stress is governed by the **Law of Laplace**. For the LV (thick-walled sphere approximation):

**wall stress (sigma) = (P x r) / (2h)**

where P = intracavitary pressure, r = cavity radius, h = wall thickness. So afterload rises with **higher pressure** (hypertension, aortic stenosis) and with a **larger radius** (ventricular dilatation), and falls with **greater wall thickness**.

[[figure:afterload-wall-stress]]

This equation explains two key adaptations and one vicious cycle:
- **Pressure overload** (HTN, AS) -> the ventricle lays down sarcomeres in parallel -> **concentric hypertrophy** (increased h) -> wall stress is normalised.
- **Volume overload** (AR, MR) -> sarcomeres in series -> **eccentric hypertrophy/dilatation** (increased r), which *raises* wall stress.
- A failing, dilated ventricle has a large r, so wall stress (and O2 demand) climbs even at normal pressures - afterload reduction (ACE inhibitors, vasodilators) breaks this cycle.
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
Arterial load has several components: mean **SVR** (steady, resistive), **arterial compliance** (pulsatile - stiff aortas raise systolic pressure and afterload), **aortic input impedance**, and any **valvular obstruction** (AS adds a fixed pressure load).

On a PV loop, **increasing afterload** raises the pressure at which the aortic valve opens, so the ventricle ejects less: **ESV rises and stroke volume falls** (the end-systolic point climbs the ESPVR up and to the right - higher end-systolic pressure at a higher ESV). The reverse - **afterload reduction** - is how vasodilators increase forward stroke volume in a failing or regurgitant ventricle.

Because wall stress is a prime determinant of **myocardial O2 demand**, afterload reduction both offloads the pump and reduces ischaemia.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body: Afterload ties blood pressure, valve disease, hypertrophy patterns and oxygen demand into one equation. Understanding sigma = Pr/2h lets you predict why pressure overload makes walls thick, why dilatation is self-perpetuating, and why "unloading" the ventricle is such a recurring therapeutic lever.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **Afterload is not simply "blood pressure" or "SVR"** - a dilated ventricle at normal BP can face high afterload because r is large.
- Do not equate afterload with preload: preload = pre-contraction stretch; afterload = the ejection load.
- In **aortic stenosis** the afterload is the valve, so **arm-cuff systolic pressure underestimates the true LV afterload** (there is a transvalvular gradient).
- Concentric hypertrophy is initially *compensatory* (lowers wall stress) but eventually causes diastolic dysfunction and ischaemia - "good then bad".
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- A Laplace calculation or "what happens to wall stress if the ventricle dilates?" -> **rises** (r up).
- "Why does concentric LVH develop in aortic stenosis?" -> to **increase h and normalise wall stress** against the pressure load.
- A PV-loop stem where the aortic-opening pressure rises -> **increased afterload, reduced SV**.
- "Drug that improves forward flow in acute mitral regurgitation?" -> an **afterload reducer** (e.g. nitroprusside).
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **Laplace: sigma = Pr/2h.** Afterload up with pressure and radius, down with thickness.
- **Concentric hypertrophy (pressure overload, e.g. AS/HTN) normalises wall stress**; dilatation raises it.
- **Increasing afterload -> higher ESV, lower SV**; decreasing it -> higher SV.
- Afterload reduction (ACEi/ARB, hydralazine, nitroprusside) is first-line haemodynamic therapy in **HFrEF, acute MR and AR**.
- Wall stress is a major driver of **myocardial oxygen demand**.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: Afterload and wall stress

sections.body:
The **cardiac cycle** is the repeating sequence of electrical and mechanical events in one heartbeat. It divides into **systole** (ventricular contraction and ejection) and **diastole** (relaxation and filling). At rest (~75 bpm) one cycle lasts ~0.8 s: systole ~0.3 s and diastole ~0.5 s. As heart rate rises, **diastole shortens first and most** - which is why tachycardia impairs filling and coronary perfusion before it impairs ejection.

The Wiggers diagram is the single most tested physiology figure in cardiology: it stacks the aortic, left-ventricular (LV) and left-atrial (LA) pressure traces, LV volume, the ECG and the heart sounds on one time axis so every event lines up.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
Read the cycle as **seven phases**. The two isovolumic phases (all four valves shut) are the anchors - no blood moves, so volume is flat and pressure changes fastest.

**Systole**
1. **Atrial systole** - the P wave has just fired; atrial contraction adds the final ~10-25% of filling ("atrial kick") and produces the **a wave**. End of this phase = **end-diastolic volume (EDV ~120 mL)** and the S4 if present.
2. **Isovolumic contraction** - QRS triggers ventricular contraction; LV pressure shoots up. When it exceeds LA pressure the **mitral valve closes (S1)**. All valves shut, volume constant. LV pressure climbs from ~10 to ~80 mmHg.
3. **Rapid ejection** - LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure, the **aortic valve opens**, and ~70% of the stroke volume leaves. LV and aortic pressures peak together at ~120 mmHg.
4. **Reduced ejection** - repolarisation (T wave) begins; ejection slows as pressures fall.

**Diastole**
5. **Isovolumic relaxation** - LV pressure drops below aortic pressure, the **aortic valve closes (S2)**, marking **end-systolic volume (ESV ~50 mL)**. The **dicrotic notch (incisura)** appears on the aortic trace. All valves shut again.
6. **Rapid filling** - LV pressure falls below LA pressure, the **mitral valve opens**, and blood rushes in passively (an S3 may occur here).
7. **Reduced filling (diastasis)** - filling slows as LV and LA pressures equalise, until the next atrial systole.

Stroke volume = EDV - ESV = ~120 - 50 = **~70 mL**; ejection fraction = SV/EDV = **~55-70%**.
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
Key pressures to memorise: **aortic 120/80 mmHg**, **LV ~120/0-10 mmHg** (systolic equals aortic when the valve is open; diastolic is the low LVEDP ~8-12 mmHg), **LA mean ~8-10 mmHg**. The **LV and aortic systolic pressures are equal during ejection** because the open aortic valve makes them one chamber.

[[figure:cardiac-cycle-wiggers]]

The same cycle plotted as pressure against volume is the **pressure-volume (PV) loop** - the most powerful way to see stroke volume, afterload and contractility at once. Trace it counter-clockwise: mitral closure (bottom right) -> isovolumic contraction (right, vertical) -> ejection (top, leftward) -> aortic closure/end-systole (top left) -> isovolumic relaxation (left, vertical) -> filling (bottom). The loop's **width is the stroke volume**; its top-left corner sits on the **ESPVR (contractility)**; its bottom-right corner on the **EDPVR (compliance)**.

[[figure:pv-loop]]
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body:
The jugular venous pulse mirrors right-atrial pressure through the cycle:
- **a wave** - atrial contraction (lost in AF; giant/cannon a waves in AV dissociation, TS, pulmonary hypertension).
- **c wave** - tricuspid bulging into the atrium during RV isovolumic contraction.
- **x descent** - atrial relaxation (blunted/absent, or replaced by systolic cv wave, in significant TR).
- **v wave** - atrial filling against a closed tricuspid valve (giant in TR).
- **y descent** - tricuspid opens and the atrium empties (steep in constriction; blunted in tamponade).
sections.title: Jugular venous pulse (JVP)

sections.body:
- **S1** - mitral + tricuspid closure; **marks the start of systole**, just after the QRS. Loud in mitral stenosis and short PR.
- **S2** - aortic (A2) then pulmonic (P2) closure; **marks the end of systole / start of diastole**. **Physiological splitting widens on inspiration** (delayed P2). Fixed splitting = ASD; paradoxical splitting = LBBB / severe AS.
- **S3** - early diastole, during rapid filling; normal in children/young adults, pathological ("ventricular gallop") in HF and volume overload.
- **S4** - late diastole, from atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle ("atrial gallop"); implies reduced compliance (LVH, ischaemia, HFpEF). **Absent in atrial fibrillation** (no organised atrial contraction).
sections.title: Heart sounds

sections.body: Every valve lesion, every murmur, every heart sound and most haemodynamic questions are just annotations on this one diagram. If you can draw the Wiggers cycle and the PV loop from memory and point to each valve event, pressure crossover and sound, you can reconstruct the physiology of aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation, tamponade and heart failure without memorising them separately.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **S2 marks the end of systole, not a diastolic event** - a classic distractor. Systole is "between S1 and S2".
- During **ejection the aortic valve is OPEN**, so LV and aortic pressures are equal; a pressure gradient across it in systole means **aortic stenosis**.
- The **a wave is atrial systole; the v wave is NOT ventricular** - it is atrial filling (passive) against a closed tricuspid valve.
- The mitral valve opens **after** S2 (isovolumic relaxation comes first) - it does not open at S2.
- An S3 is early diastole (filling); an S4 is late diastole (atrial kick) - do not swap them.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- A labelled Wiggers diagram with an arrow: identify the phase, the valve event, or which sound occurs there. Anchor on the **isovolumic phases** and the **pressure crossovers**.
- "When does the mitral valve close?" -> when **LV pressure exceeds LA pressure** (start of isovolumic contraction = S1).
- Given EDV and ESV, compute **SV and EF** in one step.
- A **systolic murmur** sits between S1 and S2; a **diastolic murmur** between S2 and S1 - timing comes straight from this cycle.
- JVP waveform questions (giant a wave, prominent v wave, steep/blunted y descent) map directly to the lesions above.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **EDV ~120 mL, ESV ~50 mL, SV ~70 mL, EF 55-70%.** LVEDP ~8-12 mmHg.
- **Isovolumic phases = all valves closed** (one at start of systole, one at start of diastole).
- Valve sequence per cycle: **MC -> AO -> AC -> MO** (mitral close, aortic open, aortic close, mitral open).
- **S1 = mitral closure = start of systole; S2 = aortic closure = end of systole.**
- The **dicrotic notch** on the aortic trace = aortic valve closure = coincides with S2.
- The **atrial kick** supplies ~20% of filling at rest and much more during tachycardia - its loss (AF) can precipitate decompensation in stiff ventricles (MS, HFpEF, HCM).
sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: The cardiac cycle (Wiggers)

sections.body:
**Cardiac output (CO)** is the volume of blood the heart pumps per minute:

**CO = heart rate (HR) x stroke volume (SV)**

Normal resting CO is **~4-8 L/min**. Indexed to body surface area it is the **cardiac index (CI) = 2.5-4.0 L/min/m2**. With SV ~70 mL and HR ~70/min, CO ~5 L/min - roughly the whole blood volume each minute.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
[[figure:cardiac-output-map]]

CO has exactly two proximate inputs - **HR** and **SV** - and SV has three - **preload, afterload and contractility**:
- **Heart rate** is set by autonomic balance at the SA node (sympathetic up, vagal down). Up to a point, raising HR raises CO; beyond ~150-170/min (or with loss of the atrial kick, or in a stiff ventricle) **diastolic filling time falls so much that SV drops and CO plateaus or falls**.
- **Stroke volume** rises with more preload (Frank-Starling), more contractility, and less afterload.

Guyton's analysis couples the heart to the circulation: the **cardiac (Starling) function curve** (CO rises as RA pressure rises) and the **vascular/venous return curve** (venous return falls as RA pressure rises) intersect at a single **operating point** that defines the actual CO and RA pressure. Shift either curve (give fluid, change contractility, vasodilate) and the operating point moves predictably.
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
CO can be measured directly with the **Fick principle**:

**CO = VO2 / (CaO2 - CvO2)**

Oxygen consumption (VO2 ~250 mL/min at rest) divided by the **arteriovenous O2 content difference** (~5 mL O2 per 100 mL blood = 50 mL/L). So CO = 250 / 50 = **5 L/min**. A *widened* a-v O2 difference (low CvO2, i.e. low mixed-venous saturation) signals a **low output state** - tissues extract more because flow is inadequate.

Other methods: **thermodilution** (pulmonary artery catheter) and **Doppler echo** (SV = LVOT area x velocity-time integral).

Definitions worth keeping together: **EF = SV/EDV (55-70%)**; **SV = EDV - ESV (~70 mL)**; **CI = CO/BSA**.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body: Cardiac output is the bottom line of the whole cardiovascular system - the number that determines tissue perfusion. Every other physiology topic (preload, afterload, contractility, heart rate, the Starling and venous-return curves, the Fick principle) feeds into this one equation, which is why examiners return to it constantly.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **Tachycardia does not guarantee higher CO** - past a threshold, lost filling time reduces SV enough that CO drops (a key point in AF with rapid ventricular response and in SVT).
- In the Fick equation use **content** (mL O2/L), not partial pressure or saturation alone.
- CO and CI are not the same - **always index** when comparing across body sizes.
- EF and CO are different: a dilated ventricle can keep CO "normal" with a **low EF** (large EDV), while a small, stiff ventricle can have **high EF but low CO** (small SV).
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- A Fick calculation: plug VO2 and the a-v O2 content difference, divide.
- "Narrow pulse pressure, cold peripheries, low SvO2" -> **low CO / high extraction**.
- A stem where increasing HR fails to raise CO -> **filling-time limitation**.
- "CO normal but EF 30%?" -> compensated by a **dilated, high-EDV ventricle**.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **CO = HR x SV**; **CI 2.5-4.0 L/min/m2**; resting CO ~5 L/min.
- SV determinants: **preload, afterload, contractility**.
- **Fick: CO = VO2 / (CaO2 - CvO2)**; a wide a-v O2 difference = **low output**.
- At very high heart rates CO **falls** because diastolic filling time (and SV) collapse.
- Mixed venous O2 saturation (SvO2, normally ~65-75%) is a bedside marker of the adequacy of CO relative to demand.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: Cardiac output and its determinants

sections.body:
**Contractility (inotropy)** is the *intrinsic* strength of ventricular contraction **at a given preload and afterload** - the heart's ability to generate force independent of loading conditions. It reflects the amount of **Ca2+** delivered to the myofilaments and their responsiveness to it.

Because it must be load-independent, the best index of contractility is the **end-systolic elastance, Ees** - the **slope of the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR)**.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
At the cellular level, inotropy is set by **intracellular Ca2+ handling**: Ca2+ entry via L-type channels triggers Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (via ryanodine receptors); more Ca2+ to troponin C -> more cross-bridges -> more force. Sympathetic **beta1 -> Gs -> adenylyl cyclase -> cAMP -> PKA** phosphorylates L-type channels, phospholamban and troponin, raising both the force (inotropy) and the speed of relaxation (**lusitropy**).

[[figure:contractility-pv]]

**Positive inotropes:** sympathetic stimulation / catecholamines, beta-agonists (dobutamine), digoxin and other Na/K-ATPase inhibitors (raise intracellular Na -> less Ca extrusion by Na/Ca exchanger), PDE-3 inhibitors (milrinone), increased heart rate (**Bowditch/Treppe** staircase), and Ca2+.
**Negative inotropes:** beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine Ca-channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem), ischaemia/hypoxia, acidosis, and most anti-arrhythmics.
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
Increased contractility **steepens the ESPVR (higher Ees)**. At the same EDV and afterload, the ventricle now empties to a **smaller ESV**, so **stroke volume, ejection fraction and dP/dt all rise**. Decreased contractility flattens the ESPVR, raising ESV and lowering SV/EF.

Other indices, each with a caveat:
- **dP/dt max** (peak rate of pressure rise in isovolumic contraction) - rises with inotropy but is **somewhat preload-dependent**.
- **Ejection fraction** - the usual clinical surrogate, but it is **load-dependent** (e.g. EF looks "preserved" in MR because the ventricle unloads into the low-pressure atrium).
- **Ees / ESPVR slope** - the reference standard, essentially **load-independent**.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body: Separating contractility from preload and afterload is the conceptual core of ventricular mechanics. It explains why inotropes help some patients and harm others, why EF can mislead, and why the ESPVR/Ees framework underlies modern understanding of heart failure and the effects of every cardioactive drug.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **Ejection fraction is NOT a pure contractility measure** - it is load-dependent (overestimated in MR, underestimated by high afterload).
- Contractility is **independent of preload** - a Frank-Starling increase in force from more stretch is **not** a change in contractility (the ventricle stays on the *same* ESPVR).
- **dP/dt max** still has some preload dependence; the ESPVR slope is the clean measure.
- A steeper ESPVR means *more* contractility - do not read the axis backwards.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Load-independent index of contractility?" -> **Ees / slope of the ESPVR**.
- A PV-loop stem where the loop narrows and ESV falls at the same EDV -> **increased contractility**.
- Mechanism of digoxin's inotropy -> **Na/K-ATPase inhibition -> raised intracellular Ca2+**.
- "Why can EF be normal in severe MR despite a sick ventricle?" -> EF is **load-dependent** (low-impedance leak into the LA).
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Contractility = force at **fixed preload and afterload**; gold-standard index = **Ees = slope of ESPVR**.
- **Increased contractility -> lower ESV, higher SV, higher EF, higher dP/dt.**
- Final common pathway is **intracellular Ca2+**; beta1 -> cAMP -> PKA is the main up-regulator.
- **Digoxin**: inhibits Na/K-ATPase -> more intracellular Na -> Na/Ca exchanger extrudes less Ca -> **positive inotropy**.
- **Force-frequency (Bowditch/Treppe):** faster rates -> stronger contractions (Ca accumulates).
sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: Contractility (inotropy)

sections.body: The **coronary circulation** perfuses the myocardium itself. The two main arteries arise from the aortic sinuses just above the valve: the **left main** (-> **LAD** and **left circumflex, LCx**) and the **right coronary artery (RCA)**. Coronary flow is unique in that **the left ventricle is perfused mainly during diastole**, and the myocardium extracts most of the oxygen delivered to it even at rest.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
**Anatomy and territories:**
- **LAD** - anterior wall, anterior 2/3 of the septum, apex (anteroseptal MI; precordial leads V1-V4).
- **LCx** - lateral wall (lateral MI; I, aVL, V5-V6).
- **RCA** - inferior wall and RV; usually supplies the **AV node (~90%)** and often the **SA node (~60%)** (inferior MI; II, III, aVF; watch for bradyarrhythmias/heart block).

**Dominance** is defined by which artery gives the **posterior descending artery (PDA)**: **right-dominant in ~85%**, left-dominant ~8%, co-dominant ~7%.

**Autoregulation:** coronary flow is kept nearly constant across a wide perfusion-pressure range (~60-140 mmHg) by **metabolic** control (adenosine, NO, hypoxia, K+/CO2) and a myogenic response. Local metabolites are the dominant minute-to-minute regulator - active hyperaemia matches flow to demand. The capacity to increase flow above resting is the **coronary flow reserve**.
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
**Why diastolic perfusion matters:** during systole the contracting LV compresses its own intramural vessels, throttling (even reversing) flow - so the LV is perfused almost entirely in **diastole**. The thin-walled RV, generating low pressure, is perfused in both systole and diastole.

[[figure:coronary-flow-diastole]]

**Coronary perfusion pressure (CPP) = aortic diastolic pressure - LV end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP).** Anything that shortens diastole (**tachycardia**), lowers aortic diastolic pressure (**hypotension, aortic regurgitation**) or raises LVEDP (**LV failure, LVH**) reduces perfusion - hitting the **subendocardium** first, because it is compressed the most and is the most ischaemia-prone layer.

**Supply vs demand:** the heart extracts **~70-75% of delivered O2 at rest** (coronary sinus SatO2 ~30%), so the extraction reserve is small - **increased demand must be met by increased coronary flow**, not more extraction.
- **Supply** = coronary flow (diastolic time, CPP, vessel patency/autoregulation) x arterial O2 content (Hb, SaO2, PaO2).
- **Demand** = **heart rate, contractility, and wall stress** (preload x radius + afterload x pressure, by Laplace).

[[figure:o2-supply-demand]]
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body: Ischaemic heart disease - angina, MI, the rationale for beta-blockers, nitrates and revascularisation - is entirely a story of **O2 supply failing to meet demand**, played out on a circulation that can only be perfused in diastole and already runs near-maximal extraction. These principles let you predict, for any clinical change, whether the myocardium will ischaemia or not.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **LV coronary flow peaks in diastole, not systole** - tachycardia harms perfusion mainly by **shortening diastole**.
- **Dominance is defined by the PDA**, not by which artery is "bigger" or supplies more muscle.
- Because extraction is near-maximal at rest, you **cannot** meet higher demand by extracting more O2 - only by **raising flow**.
- Aortic regurgitation lowers **aortic diastolic pressure -> reduced CPP** (a reason for subendocardial ischaemia even with normal coronaries).
- **Endocardium**, not epicardium, is the first and worst-hit layer in ischaemia.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Coronary perfusion pressure formula?" -> **aortic diastolic - LVEDP**.
- "Which artery supplies the AV node?" -> **RCA in ~90%** (inferior MI -> heart block).
- "Why does tachycardia cause ischaemia?" -> **shorter diastole -> less perfusion AND higher demand**.
- "Most ischaemia-prone region of the LV?" -> **subendocardium**.
- A supply/demand stem: list each lever and whether a given change (HR up, BP down, Hb down, LVH) helps or harms.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **LV perfusion is diastolic; CPP = aortic diastolic - LVEDP.**
- **Right-dominant ~85%**; dominance = who gives the **PDA**. RCA supplies the **AV node (90%)** and often SA node.
- Territories: **LAD anteroseptal, LCx lateral, RCA inferior/RV**.
- **Basal O2 extraction ~70-75%** -> little reserve -> extra demand met by **increased flow** (autoregulation, mostly adenosine/NO).
- The **subendocardium** is most vulnerable to ischaemia.
- O2 **demand** rises with HR, contractility and wall stress (the rate-pressure product HR x SBP is the usable surrogate); **supply** = coronary flow x arterial O2 content.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: Coronary circulation & myocardial O2 supply/demand

sections.body: The **Frank-Starling mechanism** (Starling's law of the heart) states that, within physiological limits, **the greater the end-diastolic stretch (preload), the greater the force of the next contraction and hence the stroke volume**. The heart intrinsically matches its output to the venous return it receives - beat to beat, and between the two ventricles - without any change in contractility or neural input.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
The mechanism is the cardiac expression of the **length-tension relationship** of the sarcomere. Stretching the myocyte toward its optimal sarcomere length (**~2.0-2.2 micrometres**):
1. improves **actin-myosin overlap** (more cross-bridges can form), and
2. - the dominant effect in cardiac muscle - increases the **Ca2+ sensitivity of troponin C** (length-dependent activation), partly through titin-mediated changes in lattice spacing.

[[figure:frank-starling]]

So more filling -> longer sarcomeres -> more force -> larger stroke volume, along a curve that **rises steeply then plateaus** (and, unlike skeletal muscle, the normal heart operates on the *ascending* limb and does not reach a true descending limb in vivo).

Changing contractility shifts the **whole curve**: positive inotropy moves it **up and to the left** (more SV for the same filling pressure); heart failure moves it **down and to the right** and flattens it, so the ventricle needs much higher filling pressures for a modest SV - which is why it congests.
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
Plotted as **stroke volume (or CO) vs LV end-diastolic pressure/volume**, the Frank-Starling curve is the cardiac function curve. On a PV loop the same idea appears as: increase EDV -> the end-systolic point rides up the **unchanged ESPVR** -> wider loop -> larger SV.

This mechanism also **equalises right and left ventricular outputs**: if the RV transiently pumps more, LV filling rises, stretching the LV and increasing its output to match - preventing pulmonary pooling.

Clinically, patients on the **steep** portion are "preload-responsive" (a fluid bolus raises SV); patients on the **flat** portion are not (fluid only raises filling pressure and causes oedema). Failing hearts sit on a depressed, flattened curve.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body: Frank-Starling is the heart's built-in self-regulation. It underlies how the circulation balances itself, how we judge fluid responsiveness in shock, and how heart failure is conceptualised as a shifted curve. It is the mechanistic bridge between preload, stroke volume and the cardiac function curve.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- A larger SV from increased preload is **Frank-Starling, not increased contractility** - contractility means a shift to a *new* curve (new ESPVR).
- There is **no clinically relevant descending limb** in the intact heart - worsening congestion in failure reflects a **depressed curve**, not "over-stretch falling off the top".
- Frank-Starling (cardiac length-tension) is distinct from the **Starling forces** (capillary filtration) - same name, different concept.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- A graph with two curves (normal vs shifted-down) -> identify **contractility change vs preload change**.
- "Fluid bolus raised the wedge pressure but not the stroke volume" -> patient is on the **flat part** (not preload-responsive).
- "How do the two ventricles keep equal outputs?" -> **Frank-Starling** auto-matching.
- Mechanism question -> **length-dependent increase in Ca2+ sensitivity / filament overlap**.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **More stretch -> more force -> more stroke volume** (length-dependent activation + better filament overlap).
- Optimal sarcomere length **~2.2 micrometres**.
- Dominant cardiac mechanism = **increased myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity**, not just overlap.
- **Preload** moves you *along* a curve; **contractility** moves the *whole curve* up/down.
- The normal heart works on the **ascending limb**; failure = depressed, flattened curve needing high filling pressures.
- It automatically **balances the outputs of the two ventricles**.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: The Frank-Starling mechanism

sections.body:
**Preload** is the degree of myocardial stretch at the end of diastole - the load on the muscle *before* it contracts. Strictly it is the **end-diastolic sarcomere length**; because we cannot measure that clinically, we approximate it with (in descending order of fidelity): **LV end-diastolic volume (LVEDV)** -> **LV end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP)** -> **pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP/PAWP)** -> central venous pressure.

More stretch -> more forceful contraction (the **Frank-Starling** mechanism). Preload is therefore the input the ventricle converts into stroke volume.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
Preload is set by how much blood returns to and fills the ventricle in diastole - i.e. by **venous return** and diastolic filling time.

Determinants that **raise** preload: increased blood/intravascular volume, increased **venous tone** (sympathetic venoconstriction mobilising the splanchnic reservoir), the **skeletal-muscle pump**, the **respiratory pump** (inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure, augmenting venous return), a longer diastole (bradycardia), and the **atrial kick**. Gravity/standing, venodilators (nitrates), hypovolaemia and tachycardia **lower** it.

Guyton framed this as **mean systemic filling pressure (MSFP ~7 mmHg)** - the pressure in the vasculature with no flow, set by volume and venous tone - driving blood back toward the right atrium. Venous return is proportional to **(MSFP - right atrial pressure) / resistance to venous return**, so a *rising* RA pressure actually *reduces* venous return (the back-pressure opposes it).
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
[[figure:preload-venous-return]]

On a PV loop, **increasing preload widens the loop to the right** (higher EDV) and - with contractility and afterload unchanged - the end-systolic point stays on the same ESPVR, so **stroke volume increases** (Frank-Starling). This is pure length-dependent activation, not a change in contractility.

Clinical surrogates and normals: **PCWP 6-12 mmHg** (estimates LA pressure and hence LVEDP when there is no mitral obstruction), **CVP/RAP 2-6 mmHg**. PCWP rises in LV failure and volume overload; it is falsely high relative to LVEDP in mitral stenosis.

Note the "Starling" name appears twice and they are different: the **Frank-Starling** law relates *cardiac* stretch to force, whereas the **Starling forces** (capillary hydrostatic vs oncotic pressures) govern transcapillary fluid filtration and oedema.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body: Preload is the "tank" the heart draws from. Half of resuscitation, diuresis, nitrate therapy and the interpretation of wedge pressures is really about moving the ventricle along its Frank-Starling curve. Separating preload (stretch/volume) from the pressures we use to estimate it prevents the commonest reasoning errors in heart failure and shock.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **Preload is a volume/stretch, not a pressure** - LVEDP only tracks it when compliance is normal. In a stiff ventricle (LVH, HFpEF) a high LVEDP/PCWP can coexist with a *normal or low* EDV.
- **PCWP overestimates LVEDP in mitral stenosis** (the obstruction holds LA pressure up).
- Do not confuse **Frank-Starling (cardiac)** with **Starling forces (capillary filtration)**.
- Giving fluids only helps if the ventricle is on the **steep** part of its Starling curve; on the flat part it just raises filling pressure and causes congestion.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Best clinical estimate of LV preload?" -> **PCWP** (then LVEDV on echo/ventriculography).
- A question that raises CVP and asks about venous return -> remember the **back-pressure effect lowers VR**.
- Nitroglycerin's main haemodynamic action -> **venodilation -> reduced preload**.
- A fluid-challenge/Starling-curve stem tests whether the patient is preload-responsive (steep part) vs congested (flat part).
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Preload = **end-diastolic stretch** ~ LVEDV; clinical index = **PCWP (6-12 mmHg)**.
- **MSFP ~7 mmHg** is the x-intercept of the venous return curve.
- **Rising RA pressure lowers venous return** (it is the back-pressure).
- Venodilators (**nitrates**) and diuretics lower preload - the basis of relieving pulmonary congestion.
- The **atrial kick** is a preload contributor; losing it (AF) matters most in stiff/non-compliant ventricles.
- Inspiration **increases** right-heart venous return (and transiently splits S2).

title: Preload and venous return

sections.body:
**Inspection and palpation of the precordium** come before auscultation and often tell you the lesion before the stethoscope does: the **apex beat** reports LV size and the type of load, a **left parasternal heave** reports the RV (or a huge left atrium), and a **thrill** is a murmur loud enough to feel.

Inspect from the foot of the bed, then palpate with the patient at 45 degrees and again in the **left lateral decubitus** position (it brings the apex against the chest wall). Use the flat of the hand for heaves, the fingertips for the apex beat and the base of the fingers (or the ulnar border of the hand) for thrills.

[[figure:pe-murmur-areas-map]]

The areas on the map are **listening posts named after where each valve's sound is best heard**, not the anatomical positions of the valves; the same landmarks are used for palpation (apex, left sternal edge, pulmonary area, aortic area).
sections.title: Definition

sections.body: **Why the apex feels different with pressure and volume loads.** A **pressure** load (AS, hypertension) causes **concentric** hypertrophy: a thick wall around a normal cavity that contracts forcefully and for longer, so the apex is **sustained (heaving)** but stays in place until the ventricle fails. A **volume** load (MR, AR, shunts) causes **eccentric** hypertrophy: a dilated cavity ejecting a large stroke volume quickly, so the apex is **displaced, diffuse and hyperdynamic (thrusting)** but brief. A stiff ventricle that depends on atrial contraction adds a palpable presystolic (S4) impulse; rapid early filling of a dilated ventricle adds a palpable S3.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body:
### Inspection

- **Scars**: median sternotomy (CABG, valve surgery), **left anterolateral thoracotomy** (closed mitral valvotomy), **left posterolateral thoracotomy** (PDA ligation, coarctation repair, Blalock-Taussig shunt), left infraclavicular (pacemaker or ICD; feel for the generator), saphenous vein harvest scars on the legs.
- **Chest shape**: pectus excavatum (can displace the apex and cause a flow murmur), kyphoscoliosis (cor pulmonale).
- **Visible pulsations**: apex, left parasternal lift, epigastric pulsation (RV in emphysema, or aorta), suprasternal pulsation (aortic aneurysm, coarctation).

### The apex beat

The **lowest and most lateral** point at which a definite outward impulse is felt. Normal: **5th left intercostal space, at or inside the midclavicular line**, the size of a coin (less than about 2.5 cm, one intercostal space), brief (it does not outlast the first part of systole).

| Character | Feel | Load or lesion |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | Brief, localised, not displaced | - |
| Heaving (sustained, pressure-loaded) | Forceful and **sustained** through systole, little or no displacement | Pressure overload: **AS**, hypertension, HCM |
| Thrusting (hyperdynamic, volume-loaded) | Forceful but brief, **displaced** down and out, diffuse | Volume overload: **MR**, **AR**, VSD, PDA |
| Tapping | Brief tap = a **palpable S1** | **Mitral stenosis** |
| Double or triple | Palpable a wave (S4) plus systolic impulse, sometimes a late systolic bulge | **HCM**, LVH with a stiff LV |
| Diffuse, dyskinetic | Large impulse over several spaces, paradoxical bulge | LV aneurysm after anterior MI, dilated cardiomyopathy |
| Impalpable | - | Obesity, emphysema, **pericardial effusion**, dextrocardia (feel on the right) |

**Displacement without LV enlargement:** mediastinal shift (tension pneumothorax, lung collapse, effusion), pectus excavatum, scoliosis.

### Heaves and thrills

- **Left parasternal heave** (the heel of the hand lifted at the lower left sternal edge): **RV hypertrophy or dilatation** (pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary stenosis, ASD, MS, cor pulmonale). A **late systolic** parasternal lift can also come from a giant left atrium expanding in severe MR and pushing the heart forward: time it.
- **Palpable P2** in the pulmonary area: pulmonary hypertension.
- **Palpable S1** at the apex: mitral stenosis (the tapping apex).
- **Palpable S3 and S4**: an early diastolic or presystolic outward movement at the apex (volume overload; stiff LV).

A **thrill** is a palpable murmur and means at least **grade 4/6**:

| Thrill site and timing | Usual cause |
|---|---|
| Aortic area and carotids, systolic | Aortic stenosis |
| Left lower sternal edge, systolic | VSD (also post-infarction VSD); obstructive HCM |
| Pulmonary area, systolic | Pulmonary stenosis |
| Apex, systolic | Severe MR (e.g. flail leaflet) |
| Apex, diastolic | Mitral stenosis (with the patient on the left side) |
| Left infraclavicular, continuous | PDA |
| Suprasternal notch, systolic | AS, coarctation |
sections.title: Physical examination

sections.body:
Read the apex and the parasternal area together:

1. **Displaced, thrusting apex + soft S1 + pansystolic murmur** -> chronic MR (volume load).
2. **Undisplaced, heaving apex + slow-rising pulse + ejection murmur with a thrill at the base** -> severe AS (pressure load).
3. **Tapping apex + left parasternal heave + palpable P2** -> MS with pulmonary hypertension.
4. **Double apical impulse + jerky pulse + murmur at the LLSB** -> obstructive HCM.
5. **Impalpable apex + quiet sounds + raised JVP + hypotension** -> pericardial effusion with tamponade.
6. **Parasternal heave + wide fixed split S2** -> ASD with RV volume load.

The apex beat in **dextrocardia** is on the right; in **situs inversus** with dextrocardia the liver dullness is on the left as well.
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
- A **heaving** apex is a **pressure** load and is usually **not** much displaced; a **thrusting**, displaced apex is a **volume** load.
- A parasternal lift in late systole may be the **left atrium** of severe MR, not RVH.
- An apex displaced by **pectus excavatum** or mediastinal shift is not cardiomegaly; percuss and check the trachea.
- A thrill always means **grade 4 or more**; you cannot have a grade 3 murmur with a thrill.
- The auscultatory "areas" are not valve positions: the mitral valve lies behind the left sternal edge at the 4th space, but its sound is best heard at the apex.
- Feel the apex in the **left lateral position** before calling it impalpable.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Tapping, undisplaced apex beat" -> mitral stenosis (palpable S1).
- "Sustained, heaving, undisplaced apex" -> pressure overload (AS, hypertension).
- "Displaced, hyperdynamic apex" -> volume overload (MR, AR).
- "Double apical impulse" -> HCM.
- "Left parasternal heave and palpable P2" -> pulmonary hypertension.
- "Systolic thrill at the left lower sternal edge after an MI, new harsh murmur" -> ventricular septal rupture.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Normal apex: 5th left intercostal space, midclavicular line, coin-sized.
- **Heaving = pressure** (AS, HTN, HCM); **thrusting/displaced = volume** (MR, AR, shunts); **tapping = MS**; **double = HCM**; **dyskinetic = LV aneurysm**.
- **Left parasternal heave** = RV pressure or volume load (PH, PS, ASD, MS).
- **Thrill = murmur grade 4 or more.**
- Left lateral thoracotomy scar in a woman from an endemic area = previous closed mitral valvotomy.

sections.body:
This guide follows the ESC 2019 pathway that the PPDS exam is built on: **stable or unstable first**, then probability, D-dimer and CTPA, then **risk class**, which decides between home treatment, monitoring and reperfusion. The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline adds its own A-E categories; they are mapped below.

*Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.*
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
[[figure:pulmonary-embolism-algorithm]]

### Scores at the bedside
| Tool | Items | How it is used |
|---|---|---|
| sPESI (1 point each) | Age >80; cancer; chronic HF or chronic lung disease; HR ≥110; SBP <100; SaO2 <90% | 0 = low 30-day mortality; ≥1 = intermediate risk |
| YEARS | Clinical signs of DVT; haemoptysis; PE most likely diagnosis | 0 items: D-dimer <1000 ng/mL excludes; ≥1 item: D-dimer <500 excludes |
| PERC (all must be absent) | Age ≥50; HR ≥100; SaO2 <95%; haemoptysis; oestrogen; prior VTE; unilateral leg swelling; recent surgery/trauma | Only for very low gestalt probability; all negative = no testing |
| Age-adjusted D-dimer | Age x 10 µg/L after 50 years | Raises specificity in older patients (ESC 2019 IIa B) |
| Wells (two-level) | DVT signs 3; PE most likely 3; HR >100 1.5; immobilisation/surgery 1.5; prior VTE 1.5; haemoptysis 1; cancer 1 | >4 = PE likely -> CTPA; ≤4 = D-dimer first |
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
### ESC 2019 early mortality risk classes
| Risk class | Haemodynamic instability | sPESI ≥1 or PESI III-V | RV dysfunction (TTE/CTPA) | Raised troponin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| High | Yes | (+) | Yes | (+) |
| Intermediate-high | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Intermediate-low | No | Yes | One or none positive | One or none positive |
| Low | No | No | No (if assessed) | No (if assessed) |

### AHA/ACC 2026 PE Categories (in brief)
| Category | Meaning | Usual setting |
|---|---|---|
| A | Asymptomatic (incidental) PE | Outpatient |
| B | Symptomatic, low severity score (e.g. sPESI 0); B1 subsegmental, B2 more proximal | Early discharge generally |
| C (C1-C3) | Elevated severity score; C1 normal RV and biomarkers, C2 abnormal RV or biomarker, C3 both abnormal | Hospital; anticoagulation |
| D1 / D2 | Incipient failure: transient hypotension / normotensive shock (lactate, AKI) | Hospital; advanced therapy may be considered |
| E1 / E2 | Persistent hypotension with cardiogenic shock / refractory shock or arrest | Systemic thrombolysis (Class 1); catheter or surgical therapy reasonable; VA-ECMO reasonable in refractory shock |
sections.title: Severity classification

sections.body:
- **High risk**: UFH + systemic thrombolysis (ESC 2019 I B); surgical embolectomy (I C) or catheter-directed therapy (IIa C) if contraindicated or failed.
- **Intermediate-high**: anticoagulation, monitoring, **rescue** thrombolysis on deterioration (I B); routine primary thrombolysis not recommended (III B).
- **Intermediate-low**: anticoagulation in hospital.
- **Low**: DOAC; early discharge if Hestia/sPESI allow (IIa A).
- Parenteral choice: LMWH or fondaparinux over UFH, except in instability or planned reperfusion.
- Oral choice: DOAC over VKA (I A); VKA for antiphospholipid syndrome and when DOACs are contraindicated.
- Duration: ≥3 months for all; stop after a major transient risk factor; extended therapy if unprovoked or persistent risk factor.
- Follow-up: ask about dyspnoea and exercise limitation at every visit for at least 1 year to detect CTEPD/CTEPH (AHA/ACC 2026).
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body: PE is the classic 'do not miss' cause of chest pain, syncope and shock, and the exam tests a single skill: matching the intensity of treatment to the risk class. Over-treating with thrombolysis kills through bleeding; under-treating high-risk PE kills through RV failure.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- Sending an **unstable** patient to CT when bedside echo would decide (normal RV practically excludes PE as the cause of shock).
- Ordering D-dimer when clinical probability is **high** (a negative result does not exclude PE): go to CTPA.
- Using a fixed 500 cut-off in an 80-year-old (use **age x 10**).
- Calling sPESI 0 with RV dysfunction 'low risk': ESC 2019 classes it **intermediate-low**.
- Routine thrombolysis in intermediate-high risk (PEITHO: bleeding and haemorrhagic stroke outweigh benefit).
- Large fluid boluses in RV failure (worsens septal shift).
- DOACs in pregnancy or antiphospholipid syndrome.
- Using echo to diagnose PE in a stable patient (AHA/ACC 2026: do not use echo to confirm or exclude PE).
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- Hypotension, raised JVP, clear lungs, RV dilated with **McConnell sign** -> high-risk PE -> thrombolysis.
- ECG S1Q3T3, sinus tachycardia, new RBBB, T inversion V1-V4 -> RV strain.
- Normotensive PE with RV/LV ≥1 and raised troponin -> **intermediate-high**: anticoagulate and monitor, not routine thrombolysis.
- Pregnant woman with suspected PE -> pregnancy-adapted YEARS, LMWH.
- 'Which DOAC needs heparin lead-in?' -> **dabigatran and edoxaban**.
- Persistent dyspnoea 3 months after PE with mismatched perfusion defects -> **CTEPH** (V/Q scan is the screening test).
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Instability definition: arrest, obstructive shock, or persistent hypotension (SBP <90 or drop ≥40 mmHg >15 min).
- RV dysfunction: RV/LV ≥1.0, TAPSE <16 mm.
- Intermediate-high = sPESI ≥1 + RV dysfunction + troponin.
- Thrombolysis: high risk (I B) and rescue (I B); not routine otherwise (III B).
- Alteplase 100 mg over 2 h.
- DOAC over VKA; LMWH over UFH unless unstable.
